Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty Images Wildfires Past fires suggest effects of Europe and North America wildfires may linger for years Three years after Maui wildfires many still struggle with ‘biological, emotional and social consequences’, study says Oliver Milman Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 00.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A spate of ferocious wildfires across North America and Europe , worsened by the climate crisis, has incinerated homes and forests and forced thousands of people to flee. Previous fires suggest the effects of these blazes may linger for years to come. The current fires and their plumes of smoke can appear to be a temporary, if immediate, crisis. Nearly 1,000 fires have sprung into life in the boreal forests of Canada, causing the evacuation of towns and toxic smoke to waft into major Canadian and US cities, prompting threats of retribution from Donald Trump, who bizarrely accused Canada of “poisoning” his country’s air. Smoke is billowing from wildfires in the US too, amid the third major heatwave of the past month which has furthered dried out parched vegetation. Vast, lightning-sparked fires across Washington, eastern Oregon and Idaho have caused a plume of smoke so large that it could reach Florida. In Europe, meanwhile, huge fires have gripped parts of the UK , France and Spain , causing the evacuation of more than 250,000 people. View image in fullscreen A house damaged by wildfires in Blagon, south-western France, on Monday. Photograph: Laurent Perpigna/EPA The climate crisis, caused by the burning of fossil fuels, is known to be creating more fire-prone conditions around the world by drying out soils and plants. “The entire Iberian peninsula is suffering the effects of the climate emergency in a very specific way,” said Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s prime minister. Scientists have also long been aware of the unhealthy consequences of wildfire smoke, which can trigger severe respiratory and cardiac problems in affected people. A recent study found that exposure to tiny particles carried in wildfire smoke will raise the risk of hospitalization for older people hundreds of miles away from fires. “The cardiovascular toll of wildfire smoke reaches well beyond the fire lines and well beyond the day the sky turns orange,” said Kai Chen, associate professor of epidemiology at the Yale School of Public Health and study co-author. But identifying the ongoing effects of wildfires long after they have been extinguished has been a more recent understanding. There are continuing challenges in Maui, the second largest of Hawaii’s islands, three years after wildfires there caused more than 100 deaths and razed several thousand buildings, a new report highlights. While living and economic conditions have generally improved since the fires, many people in Maui are still struggling with health concerns such as poorer lung functions, higher blood pressure and mental health challenges, according to the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study , led by researchers at the University of Hawaii and released on Monday. View image in fullscreen An aerial view of vegetation regrowth amid areas destroyed or damaged by the Lahaina wildfire, including the iconic banyan tree, on 4 August 2024 in Lahaina, Hawaii. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images “The progress is real, and it should be recognized,” said Alika Maunakea, co-director of the study and a school of medicine professor at the University of Hawaii. “But the biological, emotional and social consequences of a disaster do not disappear on the same timeline as debris removal or reconstruction.” Nearly half of all adults in the Maui study continued to report depressive symptoms, with nearly one in five experiencing post-traumatic stress. The study, which conducted screenings of more than 2,500 participants, also found severe depressive symptoms and post-traumatic stress increased among children and adolescents, as did blood pressure readings and obesity levels. “Children may appear resilient while still carrying significant emotional and physical effects beneath the surface,” said Christopher Knightsbridge, a mental health therapist based in Lahaina, a coastal town that was largely destroyed by the fires. “Supporting children means supporting the entire family, including their housing, food security, daily routines and access to trusted care,” he added. The researchers stressed that long-term monitoring and intervention is required following a major wildfire event due to impacts that can last for years afterwards. While the skies over North America and Europe will eventually clear of smoke after a tinderbox summer of fire, this climate change-driven era of wildfire is set to exact a lengthy toll. As well as better support for those directly affected by fires, experts say that authorities in smoke-affected areas could respond to the threat of repeated smoke exposure by creating “clean air centers” that people can flee to in order to escape smoke and other air pollutants. A research paper from last year , which found a 7% increase in mortality among a cohort of older people living in southern California over a three-year period due to wildfire smoke exposure, recommended that “activation of public health measures such as clean air centers should not only depend on intensity of smoke, as the long-term effects can be harmful, even at low levels.” Lara Schwarz, an environmental health scientist at UC Berkley who led the research, said: “As wildfires become more frequent and severe in the context of climate change, with California being at high risk, understanding how these harmful wildfires will affect us in the long term is critical to informing better public health action and response.” Explore more on these topics Wildfires France Canada Americas Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Daughter of British couple killed in Spanish wildfire rejects claim they ignored order to leave Europe burns: a visual guide to the wildfires ‘Extremely scary findings’ show climate crisis is supercharging Europe’s wildfire weather ‘We can’t make it better again’: what Europe’s wildfires tell us about the climate crisis Wildfire near Sizewell nuclear plant causes ‘total devastation’ to Suffolk landscape Race to extinguish blazes across Europe as fire weather breaks records Will brutal wildfires force French leaders to take climate crisis seriously? (AP Photo/Claudia Ciobanu) (AP Photo/Claudia Ciobanu) KONOTOPIE, Poland (AP) — An enormous statue of the Virgin Mary that is believed to be Europe's tallest was inaugurated on Saturday in a small Polish village, in the presence of legendary anti-communist leader Lech Walesa. Hundreds of people took part in the consecration of the monument, which towers 55.6 meters (182 feet) over Konotopie in central Poland, the home of fewer than 150 people. While helicopters scattered miniature red roses over the crowd, priests in white robes celebrated Mass and the popular Mazowsze folk ensemble sang and danced to traditional Polish music. Advertisement Advertisement The Polish statue is taller — if less dramatically located — than the Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, which measures some 38 meters (125 feet) including its pedestal. Its height includes a crown-shaped 15-meter (49-foot) pedestal. It also surpasses another recent large-scale religious monument in Poland, the Christ the King statue in the western town of Swiebodzin, which was unveiled in 2010 and — complete with the mound it stands on — rises some 52 meters (170 feet) above the ground. There is a taller statue of the Virgin Mary in the Philippines, which measures some 98 meters (322 feet). But the new one in Poland is believed to be the largest of its kind in Europe. An anti-communist legend celebrates Catholic Poland Walesa, who won the Nobel Peace Prize for his leadership of the Polish anti-communist resistance as the head of the Solidarity trade union, and was later Polish president, had a front row seat during the inauguration ceremony. Advertisement Advertisement "This is the end of my path," the 82-year-old Walesa told the AP, suggesting that the causes he has long championed, including democracy and Catholic faith, are now completed. "I started with the Virgin Mary and I end with the Virgin Mary." During his Solidarity days, Walesa famously wore a Black Madonna pin and has often credited his faith in God with giving him the strength to fight against communism. The vast majority of Poles identify as Catholic, and the Catholic church played a powerful role in public life after the fall of communism in 1989, benefiting from the prestige it earned through its support for the anti-communist opposition. The country is the homeland of St. John Paul II , who reigned as pope from 1978 until his death in 2005. A huge statue of him — but much smaller than the one of Mary — was unveiled over a decade ago in the city of Czestochowa. Advertisement Advertisement The influence of religion in public life has gradually declined in recent years, particularly among younger people and in urban areas. However, the Catholic church remains influential, especially in rural communities and among older generations. "I cannot help but notice the weakening of the institution of the church, a withdrawal of specific social categories from Catholicism, and this hurts me," Bishop Wiesław Mering, a Polish Roman Catholic prelate who attended the ceremony, told the AP. "The history of Christianity has ups and downs but this place is a reminder that Mary won't give up on Poland," the bishop said. Local millionaires financed massive statue to give thanks to God The statue was commissioned by local millionaires Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. The couple live in a small palace a few kilometers (miles) from Konotopie. Advertisement Advertisement Roman Karkosik, an entrepreneur whose ventures included plastic-bottle manufacturing in the 1990s, amassed a fortune through investments on the Warsaw Stock Exchange to became one of Poland's wealthiest individuals. The couple have said the monument is an expression of their gratitude to God. "The statue will be for all people," Grażyna Karkosik told AP. "Each of us coming to see it will think more deeply about their own lives, not only about God." Local authorities hope the monument will become both a major pilgrimage site and a tourist destination. The statue features a viewing platform built inside its pedestal. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd94.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Fire and smoke rise at EMCO's ammunition storage facility near Gorni Varpishta in central Bulgaria By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 2 hours ago Bulgaria is investigating the cause of an overnight fire at an ammunition storage site run by a private defence company. Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said the authorities "are not ruling out outside interference" in the incident in central Bulgaria. No-one was injured in the blaze that triggered a series of explosions. EMCO company, whose weapons are used by Ukraine against invading Russian forces, said the fire at its site was sabotage and that human error was "completely ruled out". It did not say who might be responsible. The latest incident follows last month's fire and blasts at another EMCO ammunition warehouse in the area. In a statement, EMCO said the storage facility that was burned this time - near the central village of Gorni Varpishta, some 170km (106 miles) east of the capital Sofia - had not been used for months and was inspected just 20 days ago, when full compliance with all regulations was confirmed. It cited a number of similar incidents at Bulgarian defence firms since 2011, saying that the latest was "no exception to the series of acts of sabotage against the Bulgarian defence industry". "As the EU and Nato member state most severely affected by such actions, Bulgaria must join the collective effort to prevent and neutralise these attacks," EMCO said. The firm is run by Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev, who Bulgarian prosecutors allege has already been targeted by Russian agents. This includes a poisoning attempt in 2015 of Gebrev, his son and another company employee - three Russian nationals were later charged in absentia for attempted murder. Bulgaria is a major weapons supplier to Ukraine, as it continues to repel a full-scale Russian invasion launched in 2022. And although Sofia has recently halted state-owned arms supplies to Ukraine, Bulgarian private defence companies continue such transfers. Russia appears to have recently escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe. Last week, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig's airport - a claim denied by Moscow as "absurd". There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia. Beállítom Nem szállhatott fel a Wizz Air Budapestről Bilbaóba induló W6 2413-as számú járata a Liszt Ferenc Nemzetközi Repülőtérről kedden hatóságoktól kapott biztonsági figyelmeztetés miatt – írta meg a Facebook-oldalán az AIRportal . Egy Facebookra felkerült videón látható , hogy számos kékvillogós jármű veszi körbe a repülőt. A Wizz Airbus A321neóját 16:30-kor tolták ki az állóhelyről, majd az egyik futópálya várakozóöblébe gurult, nem engedték felszállni. Ezzel párhuzamosan a 2-es futópályát lezárták, a reptér forgalma a másik pályán zajlott. A Wizz Air közölte a portállal, hogy járatának a hatóságoktól kapott biztonsági figyelmeztetés miatt meg kellett szakítania útját a futópálya felé. Közölték, a repülőtéri hatóságoktól és társszervektől kapott biztonsági információk alapján a járat személyzete a hatóságokkal együttműködve visszafordult. A Budapest Airport azt válaszolta a kérdésekre, hogy a légiforgalmi irányítás és az illetékes hatóságok jelenleg vizsgálnak egy olyan eseményről szóló jelentést, amely a Wizz Air Budapest-Bilbao járatát érintette. Az utasokat a repülőtéren kiszállították, a tranzitban várakoznak, a repülőtér pedig zavartalanul üzemel. Kérdéseinkkel megkerestük az Országos Rendőr-főkapitányságot, ami közölte, egy betelefonáló gyerek miatt fordult vissza a bilbaói járat. Bővebben erről itt olvashat .
